claim: Oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC) is one of the most common causes of cancer deaths.
source: Oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC) is one of the most common causes of cancer deaths.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Barrett's oesophagus (BO) is the only known precancerous precursor to OAC.
source: Barrett's oesophagus (BO) is the only known precancerous precursor to OAC, but our understanding about the molecular events leading to OAC development is limited.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus about the relationship between BO and OAC.

claim: There is a strong cell cycle gene expression signature in OAC compared to BO.
source: Here, we have integrated gene expression and chromatin accessibility profiles of human biopsies and identified a strong cell cycle gene expression signature in OAC compared to BO.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of gene expression and chromatin accessibility data from human biopsies as described in the manuscript.

claim: KLF5 is implicated in the transition from BO to OAC through chromatin accessibility changes.
source: Through analysing associated chromatin accessibility changes, we have implicated the transcription factor KLF5 in the transition from BO to OAC.
evidence: This is based on analysis of chromatin accessibility data presented in the manuscript.

claim: KLF5 expression is unchanged during the transition from BO to OAC.
source: Importantly, we show that KLF5 expression is unchanged during this transition, but instead, KLF5 is redistributed across chromatin to directly regulate cell cycle genes specifically in OAC cells.
evidence: This is supported by expression data comparing BO and OAC samples shown in the manuscript.

claim: KLF5 is redistributed across chromatin to directly regulate cell cycle genes specifically in OAC cells.
source: Importantly, we show that KLF5 expression is unchanged during this transition, but instead, KLF5 is redistributed across chromatin to directly regulate cell cycle genes specifically in OAC cells.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing differential KLF5 binding patterns and gene expression changes upon KLF5 depletion.

claim: High levels of the KLF5 target gene programme correlate with poorer patient survival.
source: This new KLF5 target gene programme has potential prognostic significance as high levels correlate with poorer patient survival.
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis using TCGA data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oesophageal cancer has a 5-year survival rate of 15%.
source: Oesophageal cancer is the eighth most common cancer worldwide, and its 5-year survival rate of 15% makes it the sixth most-common cause of cancer-related death (Ferlay et al., 2015; Pennathur et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Oesophageal cancer is the sixth most-common cause of cancer-related death.
source: Oesophageal cancer is the eighth most common cancer worldwide, and its 5-year survival rate of 15% makes it the sixth most-common cause of cancer-related death (Ferlay et al., 2015; Pennathur et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: OAC is the predominant subtype of oesophageal cancer in many Western countries.
source: A subtype of oesophageal cancer, oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC), is the predominant subtype in many Western countries and its incidence is rising rapidly (Coleman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The incidence of OAC is rising rapidly.
source: A subtype of oesophageal cancer, oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC), is the predominant subtype in many Western countries and its incidence is rising rapidly (Coleman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Patients with OAC often present at a late stage with advanced disease.
source: Patients with OAC often present at a late stage with advanced disease (Smyth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The accepted model of OAC development is the progression from Barrett's oesophagus to OAC through increasing stages of dysplasia.
source: The accepted model of OAC development is the progression from an intestinal metaplastic condition of the lower oesophagus, known as Barrett's oesophagus (BO), to OAC through increasing stages of dysplasia (Burke and Tosh, 2012; Spechler and Souza, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature describing the established model.

claim: Many mutations found in OAC are also present in BO, especially TP53.
source: Many mutations found in OAC are also present in BO, especially TP53, which suggests a stepwise transition to OAC (Ross-Innes et al., 2015; Stachler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published genomic studies.

claim: Focal amplifications largely occur in OAC compared to BO.
source: Focal amplifications differ as they largely occur in OAC compared to BO (Lin et al., 2012; Stachler et al., 2015; Yamamoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published genomic studies.

claim: The RAS-ERK signalling pathway and GATA transcription factors are the most common amplified genes in OAC.
source: The amplified genes can be grouped into functional biological pathways with the RAS-ERK signalling pathway (e.g. ERBB2; EGFR; KRAS) and GATA transcription factors (GATA4; GATA6) being the most common (Frankell et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published genomic studies.

claim: The morphology of BO differs from the oesophageal epithelia by the presence of a columnar epithelium and secretory goblet cells, rather than squamous epithelium.
source: The morphology of BO differs from the oesophageal epithelia by the presence of a columnar epithelium and secretory goblet cells, rather than squamous epithelium (reviewed in Spechler and Souza, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Mutations in TP53 are more frequent in BO from patients that had progressed to OAC.
source: Mutations in TP53 are more frequent in BO from patients that had progressed to OAC (Stachler et al., 2018) and SMAD4 mutations appear to occur exclusively in OAC, although at a low frequency (Weaver et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: SMAD4 mutations appear to occur exclusively in OAC, although at a low frequency.
source: Mutations in TP53 are more frequent in BO from patients that had progressed to OAC (Stachler et al., 2018) and SMAD4 mutations appear to occur exclusively in OAC, although at a low frequency (Weaver et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Increased TGFβ signalling through SMAD2/3 promotes growth in OAC cells.
source: Increased TGFβ signalling through other SMAD family members, SMAD2/3, promotes growth in OAC cells (Blum et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Increased expression and increased activity of AP-1 transcription factors occurs in the transition from BO to OAC.
source: Additionally, increased expression and increased activity of AP-1 transcription factors occurs in the transition from BO to OAC (Blum et al., 2019; Britton et al., 2017; Maag et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Changes to the chromatin landscape have been implicated in many cancers.
source: Changes to the chromatin landscape have been implicated in many cancers and chromatin accessibility changes during tumourigenesis are a major factor in altering regulatory element activity (Britton et al., 2017; Corces et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2015; Denny et al., 2016; Kelso et al., 2017; Rendeiro et al., 2016; Tome-Garcia et al., 2018; Zhou and Guo, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: 905 genes are differentially expressed between BO and OAC (±1.5 x; Q-value <0.05).
source: Performing differential gene expression analysis, we identified 905 differentially expressed genes between BO and OAC (±1.5 x; Q-value <0.05; Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of RNA-seq data from BO and OAC samples, with results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Of the 905 differentially expressed genes, 465 are upregulated in OAC and 440 are downregulated in OAC compared to BO.
source: Of these 905 genes, 465 are upregulated in OAC and 440 are downregulated in OAC compared to BO.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Genes upregulated in OAC from the discovery dataset were significantly upregulated in the validation dataset.
source: Genes that were upregulated in OAC from the discovery dataset were significantly upregulated in the validation dataset and likewise for downregulated in OAC genes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on validation RNA-seq data from an independent sample collection, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 'G2M checkpoint' and 'E2F1 targets' are the most significant upregulated gene sets in OAC.
source: Firstly, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) uncovered two cell cycle associated terms, 'G2M checkpoint' and 'E2F1 targets', as the most significant upregulated gene sets in OAC (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of differentially expressed genes, with results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 'Fatty acid metabolism' and 'p53 pathway' are the most significant downregulated gene sets in OAC.
source: Conversely, 'Fatty acid metabolism' and 'p53 pathway' are the most significant downregulated gene sets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of differentially expressed genes, with results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Upregulated genes in OAC are enriched in cell cycle associated terms such as 'Nuclear division', 'Regulation of mitotic cell cycle' and 'DNA replication'.
source: Secondly, biological pathway gene ontology analysis of upregulated genes revealed many cell cycle associated terms, such as 'Nuclear division', 'Regulation of mitotic cell cycle' and 'DNA replication' (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on GO term analysis of upregulated genes, with results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CDC25B, CENPI and E2F1 all showed significant upregulation in OAC compared to BO in both datasets.
source: Example genes such as CDC25B, CENPI and E2F1 all showed significant upregulation in OAC compared to BO in both datasets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data from both discovery and validation datasets, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Downregulated genes in OAC are enriched in metabolic associated terms such as 'alcohol metabolic process', 'monocarboxylic acid metabolic process' and 'Lipid catabolic process'.
source: Downregulated genes uncovered metabolic associated terms, such as 'alcohol metabolic process', 'monocarboxylic acid metabolic process' and 'Lipid catabolic process' (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on GO term analysis of downregulated genes, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IDI1, ADH4 and CIDEC all show significant downregulation in both datasets.
source: Representative example genes from these pathways such as IDI1, ADH4 and CIDEC all show significant downregulation in both datasets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data from both discovery and validation datasets, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: 35,220 accessible regions were identified within +/- 250 kb of a TSS of a differentially expressed gene.
source: After merging so that only unique peaks remained, 35,220 regions were used for further analyses (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq peak calling and merging from BO and OAC samples.

claim: 1495 regions were significantly differentially accessible between BO and OAC (±2 x; Q-value <0.1).
source: A total of 1495 regions were significantly differentially accessible (±2 x; Q-value <0.1), the majority of which increased in accessibility (1327/1495).
evidence: This is based on differential accessibility analysis of ATAC-seq data from BO and OAC samples.

claim: The majority of differentially accessible regions increased in accessibility (1327/1495).
source: A total of 1495 regions were significantly differentially accessible (±2 x; Q-value <0.1), the majority of which increased in accessibility (1327/1495).
evidence: This is based on differential accessibility analysis of ATAC-seq data.

claim: Within the KRT19 locus, both gene promoters (14%; 1/7) and distal regulatory regions (86%; 6/7) gain accessibility in OAC.
source: Within this locus, both gene promoters (14%; 1/7) and distal regulatory regions (86%; 6/7) gain accessibility in OAC.
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data at the KRT19 locus shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TCGA-ESCA samples showed similar open chromatin peak profiles and clustered with OAC samples with the exception of one sample.
source: TCGA-ESCA samples showed similar open chromatin peak profiles and clustered with our OAC samples with the exception of one sample, which clusters with our BO samples (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of ATAC-seq data from TCGA samples and the study's samples, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Regions that become more accessible in OAC contain significantly enriched motifs for AP-1, KLF, TBX, NFκB and p53 transcription factor families.
source: De novo motif discovery of regions that become more accessible in OAC contain significantly enriched motifs for AP-1, KLF, TBX, NFκB and p53 transcription factor families (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on de novo motif discovery analysis of differentially accessible regions, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AP-1 and KLF were the most frequent motifs in the differential regions and showed the strongest match score for the consensus motif.
source: AP-1 and KLF were clearly the most frequent motifs in the differential regions and showed the strongest match score for the consensus motif.
evidence: This is based on motif discovery analysis results.

claim: Motifs for KLF and AP-1 transcription factors showed the highest footprinting score in OAC in differential accessible regions.
source: In differential accessible regions, motifs for KLF (e.g. KLF4, KLF5 and KLF1) and AP-1 (e.g. FOS, JUNB, JUND, JUN and FOSL1/2) transcription factors showed the highest footprinting score in OAC, whereas motifs for homeobox transcription factors (e.g. HNF1A, HOXA5 and NKX2-5), ARID3A and MEF transcription factors (e.g. MEF2A and MEF2C) showed more footprinting in BO.
evidence: This is based on footprinting analysis of ATAC-seq data, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both FOS (AP-1) and KLF4 (KLF) motifs show a clear increase in footprint depth in OAC, indicative of more transcription factor binding.
source: Both FOS (AP-1) and KLF4 (KLF) motifs show a clear increase in footprint depth in OAC, indicative of more transcription factor binding (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq footprinting analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: KLF5 has been previously implicated in oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma as a tumour suppressor.
source: KLF5 has been previously implicated in oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma as a tumour suppressor (Tarapore et al., 2013) and has been identified as pro-tumorigenic in gastric cancer via amplifications (Chia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF5 has been identified as pro-tumorigenic in gastric cancer via amplifications.
source: KLF5 has been previously implicated in oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma as a tumour suppressor (Tarapore et al., 2013) and has been identified as pro-tumorigenic in gastric cancer via amplifications (Chia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: OE19 cells have a similar chromatin landscape to OAC biopsies.
source: To determine the gene regulatory functions of KLF5, we carried out siRNA-mediated knockdowns of KLF5 in OE19 cells, a cell line we identified as having a similar chromatin landscape to OAC biopsies (Rogerson et al., 2019) and exhibits strong tumourigenic properties (Hassan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: OE19 cells exhibit strong tumourigenic properties.
source: To determine the gene regulatory functions of KLF5, we carried out siRNA-mediated knockdowns of KLF5 in OE19 cells, a cell line we identified as having a similar chromatin landscape to OAC biopsies (Rogerson et al., 2019) and exhibits strong tumourigenic properties (Hassan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Knockdown of KLF5 resulted in 4934 genes with significant changes in gene expression (±1.3 x; Q-value <0.05).
source: Carrying out differential expression analysis identified 4934 genes (2637 upregulated and 2297 downregulated) with significant changes in gene expression (±1.3 x; Q-value <0.05; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis following siRNA-mediated KLF5 knockdown in OE19 cells.

claim: 21% (97/465) of the genes upregulated in OAC significantly overlap with those downregulated with siKLF5.
source: 21% (97/465) of the genes upregulated in OAC significantly overlap with those downregulated with siKLF5 (Figure 3E) and many of these are associated with cell cycle related functions, including genes encoding core cell cycle proteins like CCNE1, E2F1 and various MCM proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis between differentially expressed genes in OAC and genes affected by KLF5 knockdown, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Many of the genes that overlap between OAC upregulated and siKLF5 downregulated are associated with cell cycle related functions.
source: 21% (97/465) of the genes upregulated in OAC significantly overlap with those downregulated with siKLF5 (Figure 3E) and many of these are associated with cell cycle related functions, including genes encoding core cell cycle proteins like CCNE1, E2F1 and various MCM proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the overlapping gene set and their functions.

claim: KLF5 ChIP-seq in OE19 cells resulted in 13,542 peaks.
source: We therefore took the overlap of peaks between biological replicates forward for downstream analyses, resulting in 13,542 peaks (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data for KLF5 in OE19 cells.

claim: KLF5 ChIP-seq peaks are highly enriched in the KLF5 motif.
source: These peaks are highly enriched in the KLF5 motif, demonstrating the validity of the dataset, and also in AP1(FRA1) and GATA (GATA6) motifs, which we have previously revealed in genome wide studies as implicated in OAC (Britton et al., 2017; Rogerson et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of KLF5 ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: 97% of the 97 genes upregulated in OAC and downregulated after KLF5 depletion have a KLF5 ChIP-seq peak within 0.5 Mb of the TSS.
source: Focussing on the 97 genes that are upregulated in OAC and also downregulated after KLF5 depletion, 97% have a KLF5 ChIP-seq peak within 0.5 Mb of the TSS and the median distance between a KLF5 ChIP-seq peak and the TSS of all significantly downregulated genes was 11,975 bp (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq and gene expression data.

claim: The median distance between a KLF5 ChIP-seq peak and the TSS of all significantly downregulated genes was 11,975 bp.
source: Focussing on the 97 genes that are upregulated in OAC and also downregulated after KLF5 depletion, 97% have a KLF5 ChIP-seq peak within 0.5 Mb of the TSS and the median distance between a KLF5 ChIP-seq peak and the TSS of all significantly downregulated genes was 11,975 bp (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on distance analysis between KLF5 ChIP-seq peaks and gene TSSs.

claim: KLF5 expression does not increase in the transition from BO to OAC.
source: We first asked whether KLF5 expression changes in the transition from BO to OAC, however no increase in expression was found (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data comparing BO and OAC samples, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CP-A cells are derived from non-dysplastic BO and do not exhibit strong tumourigenic properties.
source: CP-A cells are derived from non-dysplastic BO and do not exhibit strong tumourigenic properties (Lin et al., 2012) so we compared KLF5 expression in BO-derived CP-A and OAC-derived OE19 cells and found that KLF5 is expressed at similar levels in (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF5 is expressed at similar levels in CP-A and OE19 cells.
source: CP-A cells are derived from non-dysplastic BO and do not exhibit strong tumourigenic properties (Lin et al., 2012) so we compared KLF5 expression in BO-derived CP-A and OAC-derived OE19 cells and found that KLF5 is expressed at similar levels in (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data comparing KLF5 protein levels in CP-A and OE19 cells.

claim: KLF5 ChIP-seq in CP-A cells resulted in 13,526 peaks.
source: We took the overlap of peaks between biological replicates forward for downstream analyses, resulting in 13,526 peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data for KLF5 in CP-A cells.

claim: Differential binding analysis revealed 8608 peaks show more binding in OE19 cells (40%), 9230 peaks are shared between the two cell-lines (44%) and 3515 show more binding in CP-A cells (16%).
source: Differential binding analysis revealed an altered KLF5 binding profile between CP-A and OE19 cells (Figure 4B,C; Supplementary file 5): 8608 peaks show more binding in OE19 cells (40%), 9230 peaks are shared between the two cell-lines (44%) and 3515 show more binding in CP-A cells (16%).
evidence: This is based on differential binding analysis of KLF5 ChIP-seq data from CP-A and OE19 cells.

claim: Regions bound by KLF5 in OE19 cells are enriched in motifs for KLF, GATA, Forkhead, AP-1 and TCF transcription factors.
source: Regions that are bound by KLF5 in OE19 cells are enriched in motifs for KLF, GATA, Forkhead, AP-1 and TCF transcription factors, whereas regions bound by KLF5 in CP-A cells are enriched for a different set of motifs with, TEAD, RUNX and p53 transcription factor families in addition to KLF and AP-1 motifs detected (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of differentially bound KLF5 regions, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Regions bound by KLF5 in CP-A cells are enriched for TEAD, RUNX and p53 transcription factor families in addition to KLF and AP-1 motifs.
source: Regions that are bound by KLF5 in OE19 cells are enriched in motifs for KLF, GATA, Forkhead, AP-1 and TCF transcription factors, whereas regions bound by KLF5 in CP-A cells are enriched for a different set of motifs with, TEAD, RUNX and p53 transcription factor families in addition to KLF and AP-1 motifs detected (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of differentially bound KLF5 regions, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Regions specifically bound by KLF5 in OAC cells exhibited increased accessibility in OE19 cells and in OAC tissue.
source: Regions specifically bound by KLF5 in OAC cells also exhibited increased accessibility in OE19 cells and importantly, accessibility is also elevated around these binding sites in OAC tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data from cell lines and patient tissue, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: OE19-specific KLF5-binding events are associated with genes involved in 'cell division' control.
source: OE19-specific KLF5-binding events are associated with genes involved in 'cell division' control, whereas CP-A-specific KLF5 binding is associated with 'epithelial cell differentiation' (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on GO term analysis of genes associated with cell-type-specific KLF5 peaks.

claim: CP-A-specific KLF5 binding is associated with 'epithelial cell differentiation'.
source: OE19-specific KLF5-binding events are associated with genes involved in 'cell division' control, whereas CP-A-specific KLF5 binding is associated with 'epithelial cell differentiation' (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on GO term analysis of genes associated with cell-type-specific KLF5 peaks.

claim: There are 371 OE19-specific KLF5-binding peaks within a 0.5 Mb locus centred on the TSS of the 97 genes upregulated in OAC and downregulated by KLF5 depletion.
source: To relate specific KLF5-binding events to gene expression changes, we took the set of 97 genes that are upregulated in OAC and downregulated by KLF5 depletion (i.e. activated by KLF5; Figure 3E) and found that there are 371 OE19-specific KLF5-binding peaks within a 0.5 Mb locus centred on the TSS.
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq and gene expression data.

claim: 257/371 of the OE19-specific KLF5 peaks contain KLF5 binding motifs.
source: We detected KLF5 binding motifs in 257/371 of these regions, and strikingly, 56% (145/257) of the peaks also house a mixture of FOXA, AP-1, GATA and TCF motifs, in addition to the KLF motif (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of OE19-specific KLF5 peaks.

claim: 56% (145/257) of the KLF5 motif-containing peaks also house a mixture of FOXA, AP-1, GATA and TCF motifs.
source: We detected KLF5 binding motifs in 257/371 of these regions, and strikingly, 56% (145/257) of the peaks also house a mixture of FOXA, AP-1, GATA and TCF motifs, in addition to the KLF motif (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There is extensive co-binding of GATA6 at OE19-specific KLF5 sites but no evidence of co-binding with HNF4A.
source: We therefore compared ChIP-seq profiles for these transcription factors, and see extensive co-binding of GATA6 at these sites but no evidence of co-binding with HNF4A (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq data for KLF5, GATA6, and HNF4A.

claim: Depletion of KLF5 and GATA6 leads to a large significant overlap in downregulated genes.
source: Finally, the predicted target gene co-regulation by KLF5 and GATA6 was validated by depletion of each factor in OE19 cells, which leads to a large significant overlap in downregulated genes (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data following siRNA-mediated knockdown of KLF5 and GATA6, shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Depletion of KLF5 in CP-A cells had little effect on cell cycle genes.
source: As expected from the lower KLF5-binding levels in these cells, depletion of KLF5 had little effect on these genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), consistent with a newly acquired function in OAC cells.
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR data following KLF5 knockdown in CP-A cells.

claim: The 371 KLF5-bound regions associated with KLF sensitive genes cluster into two groups based on chromatin accessibility patterns.
source: To establish whether the 371 KLF5-bound regions that are associated with KLF sensitive genes are relevant to OAC, we turned back to our ATAC-seq data and clustered the data to reveal two clusters. One set of regions is already partially open in CP-A cells that increase in accessibility in OE19 cells (cluster 1) and another set are closed in CP-A cells and become more accessible (cluster 2) (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2F, left).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of ATAC-seq data at KLF5-bound regions, shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The same pattern of accessibility is evident using ATAC-seq signal from BO and OAC tissue.
source: Importantly, the same pattern of accessibility is evident using ATAC-seq signal from BO and OAC tissue (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2F, right).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data from patient tissue samples.

claim: The most striking difference between cluster 1 and cluster 2 is the large proportion of AP1 motifs specifically associated with cluster one.
source: The most common motif in both clusters were KLF motifs and the most striking difference is the large proportion of AP1 motifs specifically associated with cluster one suggesting a potential role for AP1 in priming binding of KLF5 to these regions.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of the two clusters.

claim: 32% of OAC have an ERBB2 amplification.
source: Genomic amplifications in signalling receptors are common in OAC, such as ERBB2 (32% OAC have an ERBB2 amplification; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2017) and occur during the transition from BO to OAC (Stachler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to TCGA data.

claim: ERBB2 amplifications occur during the transition from BO to OAC.
source: Genomic amplifications in signalling receptors are common in OAC, such as ERBB2 (32% OAC have an ERBB2 amplification; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2017) and occur during the transition from BO to OAC (Stachler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: OE19 cells contain an amplification of the ERBB2 locus.
source: OE19 cells contain an amplification of the ERBB2 locus (Dahlberg et al., 2004) and are dependent on ERBB2 for their proliferation (Hong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: OE19 cells are dependent on ERBB2 for their proliferation.
source: OE19 cells contain an amplification of the ERBB2 locus (Dahlberg et al., 2004) and are dependent on ERBB2 for their proliferation (Hong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Differential accessibility analysis following ERBB2 depletion identified 717 regions with decreased chromatin accessibility and 733 regions with increased accessibility.
source: We performed differential accessibility analysis, which identified 717 regions with decreased chromatin accessibility and 733 regions with increased accessibility (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data following siRNA-mediated ERBB2 knockdown in OE19 cells.

claim: The majority of regions with reduced chromatin accessibility following ERBB2 depletion contain AP-1-binding motifs.
source: De novo motif analysis of the regions that exhibit reduced chromatin accessibility following ERBB2 depletion, revealed that the majority contain AP-1-binding motifs as expected from the established connections between ERK pathway signalling and AP1 transcription factors.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of differentially accessible regions following ERBB2 knockdown.

claim: The binding motif for KLF transcription factors was detected in a subset of regions with reduced chromatin accessibility following ERBB2 depletion.
source: However, the binding motif for KLF transcription factors was also detected, albeit in a subset of the regions (Figure 5B; Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Regions with reduced chromatin accessibility following ERBB2 depletion show increased chromatin accessibility in OAC tissue compared to BO.
source: These regions are relevant in the context of OAC as they also show increased chromatin accessibility in OAC tissue compared to BO (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data from patient tissue samples, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: RNA-seq following ERBB2 knockdown resulted in 778 genes down- and 664 genes up-regulated (two-fold change; FDR < 0.05, FPKM > 1).
source: The RNA-seq data were highly reproducible (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and resulted in 778 genes down- and 664 genes up-regulated (two-fold change; FDR < 0.05, FPKM > 1) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data following siRNA-mediated ERBB2 knockdown.

claim: There is a large, statistically significant overlap between directly activated KLF5 target genes and genes downregulated by ERBB2 depletion.
source: There is a large, statistically significant overlap between directly activated KLF5 target genes and genes downregulated by ERBB2 depletion.
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis between KLF5 target genes and ERBB2-regulated genes.

claim: The majority of the directly activated KLF5 target genes were reduced upon ERBB2 knockdown.
source: Moreover, a closer comparison reveals that the expression of the majority of the directly activated KLF5 target genes was reduced upon ERBB2 knockdown (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CP-A cells stably overexpressing ERBB2 exhibit high levels of ERBB2 expression and maintain ERK and AKT activation in serum starved conditions.
source: These cells exhibit high levels of ERBB2 expression, maintain ERK and AKT activation in serum starved conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and exhibit growth factor-independent proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: CP-A cells stably overexpressing ERBB2 exhibit growth factor-independent proliferation.
source: These cells exhibit high levels of ERBB2 expression, maintain ERK and AKT activation in serum starved conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), and exhibit growth factor-independent proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on growth assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Several cell cycle related genes that are activated by KLF5 in OAC cells are also activated by ERBB2 overexpression in BO cells.
source: Several cell cycle related genes that are activated by KLF5 in OAC cells are also activated by ERBB2 overexpression in BO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: ERBB2 overexpression in CP-A cells does not increase KLF5 occupancy at KLF5-binding regions associated with cell cycle genes.
source: However, we were unable to detect any increases in KLF5 occupancy at a panel of KLF5-binding regions associated with cell cycle genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Depletion of KLF5 in OE19 cells significantly impeded cell growth.
source: We first depleted KLF5 in OE19 cells using siRNA which resulted in the reduction of KLF5 protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), and the growth of cells was significantly impeded after siKLF5 treatment (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on crystal violet growth assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CRISPRi knockdown of KLF5 significantly reduced the growth of OE19 cells.
source: CRISPRi knockdown of KLF5 also significantly reduced the growth of OE19 cells (Figure 5F), mirroring the result with siKLF5.
evidence: This is based on crystal violet growth assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The growth of OE19 cells was significantly reduced with the treatment of siRNA against CCNE1, KIF14 and CLSPN.
source: The growth of OE19 cells was significantly reduced with the treatment of siRNA against CCNE1, KIF14 and CLSPN (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is based on crystal violet growth assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Knockdown of CCNE1, KIF14, and CLSPN significantly altered cell cycle patterns.
source: Knockdown of these genes also significantly altered cell cycle patterns, particularly knockdown of CLSPN which induced a prominent S-phase block (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is based on cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Knockdown of CLSPN induced a prominent S-phase block.
source: Knockdown of these genes also significantly altered cell cycle patterns, particularly knockdown of CLSPN which induced a prominent S-phase block (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is based on cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Patients with high expression of KLF5 showed no difference in survival compared to those with low expression.
source: Those with a higher expression of KLF5 showed no difference in patient survival, whereas patients with high target gene expression exhibited a significantly lower survival rate compared to those with low expression.
evidence: This is based on survival analysis using TCGA data.

claim: Patients with high expression of KLF5 target genes exhibited a significantly lower survival rate compared to those with low expression.
source: Those with a higher expression of KLF5 showed no difference in patient survival, whereas patients with high target gene expression exhibited a significantly lower survival rate compared to those with low expression.
evidence: This is based on survival analysis using TCGA data.

claim: CLSPN expression alone is predictive of increased patient survival.
source: It is noteworthy that CLSPN expression alone is predictive of increased patient survival (Figure 5H) and its enhanced expression in OAC compared to BO makes this a useful potential biomarker (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: CLSPN shows enhanced expression in OAC compared to BO.
source: It is noteworthy that CLSPN expression alone is predictive of increased patient survival (Figure 5H) and its enhanced expression in OAC compared to BO makes this a useful potential biomarker (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is based on expression data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Cell cycle deregulation is one of the key hallmarks of cancer.
source: Cell cycle deregulation is one of the key hallmarks of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011) and here we uncovered a cell cycle gene expression signature, comprised of genes that are overexpressed in OAC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a seminal review article.

claim: Recent research identified the cell-cycle as a perturbed pathway in OAC and suggested the possibility of CDK4/6 inhibitors as a therapeutic treatment.
source: Recent research identified the cell-cycle as a perturbed pathway in OAC and suggested the possibility of CDK4/6 inhibitors as a therapeutic treatment (Frankell et al., 2019; Mourikis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent published studies.

claim: FOXM1 is a key regulator of late cell cycle gene expression in OAC.
source: We have previously uncovered a deregulated FOXM1 regulatory network active in OAC, a key regulator of late cell cycle gene expression (Wiseman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: KLF5 has a tumour promoting function in pancreatic cancer.
source: KLF5 has been shown to have a tumour promoting function in pancreatic (He et al., 2018) and basal-like breast cancer (Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF5 has a tumour promoting function in basal-like breast cancer.
source: KLF5 has been shown to have a tumour promoting function in pancreatic (He et al., 2018) and basal-like breast cancer (Qin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF5 is frequently amplified in gastric cancer.
source: KLF5 is also frequently amplified in gastric cancer (Chia et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018) and has recently been shown to regulate gene expression in OAC in combination with other transcription factors, GATA6, ELF3 and EHF (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: KLF5 regulates gene expression in OAC in combination with GATA6, ELF3 and EHF.
source: KLF5 is also frequently amplified in gastric cancer (Chia et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018) and has recently been shown to regulate gene expression in OAC in combination with other transcription factors, GATA6, ELF3 and EHF (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent published study.

claim: KLF5 was identified as a master transcription factor on which OAC cell-lines were dependent.
source: This was reinforced by a recent study that identified KLF5 as a master transcription factor on which OAC cell-lines were dependent (Reddy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent published study.

claim: KLF5 has a tumour suppressor role in breast cancer.
source: Paradoxically, KLF5 has been shown to have a tumour suppressor role in oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (Tarapore et al., 2013) and breast cancer (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF4 expression is reduced in progression from BO to OAC.
source: The expression of the related protein, KLF4, together with three other genes, was able to stratify OAC from BO, albeit KLF4 expression is reduced in progression from BO to OAC (Maag et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF5 binds to a CCNE1 promoter proximal element in bladder cancer cells.
source: For example, KLF5 binds to a CCNE1 promoter proximal element in bladder cancer cells (Pattison et al., 2016) and KLF5 increases the expression of Ccnb1 and Mcm2 downstream of oncogenic Ras in fibroblasts (Nandan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF5 increases the expression of Ccnb1 and Mcm2 downstream of oncogenic Ras in fibroblasts.
source: For example, KLF5 binds to a CCNE1 promoter proximal element in bladder cancer cells (Pattison et al., 2016) and KLF5 increases the expression of Ccnb1 and Mcm2 downstream of oncogenic Ras in fibroblasts (Nandan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Claspin has recently been shown to have a broader role in cancer cell viability by protecting cancer cells from replication stress.
source: Indeed, this is exemplified by CLSPN which may have therapeutic potential as its gene product, Claspin, has recently been shown to have a broader role in cancer cell viability by protecting cancer cells from replication stress (Bianco et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent published study.

claim: KLF5 directly binds and regulates core cell cycle genes such as CDC25B, CCNE1 and MCM2.
source: KLF5 directly binds and regulates core cell cycle genes for example CDC25B, CCNE1 and MCM2, some of which are cell cycle transcription factors for example E2F1, MYBL2, thus providing a mechanism for propagating its effects on cell cycle control.
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq and gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: KLF5 binds with GATA6 in OAC.
source: This is in keeping with our finding that there is extensive overlap between the binding of KLF5 and GATA6 which is reinforced by recent studies that show that KLF5 binds with GATA6 in OAC (Chen et al., 2020) and gastric cancer (Chia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent published studies.

claim: KLF5 binds with GATA6 in gastric cancer.
source: This is in keeping with our finding that there is extensive overlap between the binding of KLF5 and GATA6 which is reinforced by recent studies that show that KLF5 binds with GATA6 in OAC (Chen et al., 2020) and gastric cancer (Chia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF5 cooperates with TEAD transcription factors, downstream of YAP/TAZ.
source: In other contexts, KLF5 has been shown to cooperate with TEAD transcription factors, downstream of YAP/TAZ (Wang et al., 2015) and KLF5 is stabilised by YAP in breast cancer cells (Zhi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF5 is stabilised by YAP in breast cancer cells.
source: In other contexts, KLF5 has been shown to cooperate with TEAD transcription factors, downstream of YAP/TAZ (Wang et al., 2015) and KLF5 is stabilised by YAP in breast cancer cells (Zhi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: KLF5 is repurposed in OAC cells and its chromatin-binding profile is massively rewired to drive increased expression of cell cycle associated genes.
source: Here, we demonstrate that there are marked changed in chromatin accessibility and associated gene expression, indicating active changes at the chromatin level during carcinogenesis. One of the major contributing factors to this change is the transcription factor KLF5. KLF5 is re-purposed in OAC cells and its chromatin-binding profile is massively rewired to drive increased expression of cell cycle associated genes (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence including ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and gene expression data.

claim: The rewiring of KLF5 results in the loss of KLF5 binding to many regulatory regions occupied in Barrett's cells.
source: Conversely, this rewiring results in the loss of KLF5 binding to many regulatory regions occupied in Barrett's cells.
evidence: This is based on differential binding analysis of KLF5 ChIP-seq data from CP-A and OE19 cells.

claim: The loss of KLF5 binding to Barrett's-specific regions is potentially associated with the loss of cell identity.
source: This loss is potentially associated with the loss of cell identity, and may also contribute to the development of the cancer phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the association of CP-A-specific KLF5 binding with epithelial cell differentiation genes.
